fetched_contents.text: Review: Adaptation of animals to heat stress Implications A systematic assessment of heat stress impacts on livestock adaptation is needed to identify the appropriate biomarkers to quantify heat stress responses in domestic livestock. Such an approach may identify both phenotypic and genotypic traits, which may be useful indicators of heat stress susceptibility or tolerance in different livestock species. These biomarkers may be included in the breeding programmes in an effort to develop thermo-tolerant breeds using marker-assisted selection. Such efforts may help to identify the appropriate agro-ecological zone specific breeds. This may provide a mechanism for sustained livestock production in the changing climate scenario. Introduction Among the environmental variables affecting animals, heat stress is one of the factors making animal production challenging in many parts of the world (El-Tarabany et al., 2017). Although animals can adapt to climatic stressors, the response mechanisms that ensure survival are also detrimental to performance (Pragna et al., 2018). The vulnerability of livestock to heat stress varies according to species, genetic potential, life stage, management or production system and nutritional status (Das et al., 2016). Moreover, under the testing environmental conditions animal productivity is affected resulting in economic losses for livestock industries. It is important that efforts to understand the adaptive responses of the domestic livestock are taken. This may pave the way for identification of various biological markers that can be used to quantify heat stress responses. Identified markers may then be incorporated into breeding programmes in an attempt to develop thermo-tolerant breeds’ specific to different agro-ecological zones. The various impacts of climate change on dairy cattle are presented in Figure 1. Heat stress was found to influence most of the productive functions in livestock (Figure 1). This is very crucial for the adaptive processes as generally the animals try to deviate the energy from the productive pathway to support vital adaptive mechanisms (Nardone et al., 2010). Heat stress affects the growth performance (Baumgard et al., 2012), milk production (Das et al., 2016), reproductive performance (Rhoads et al., 2009), meat production (Archana et al., 2018) and disease occurrences (Rojas-Downing et al., 2017). The adverse impacts of heat stress on these productive functions depend on species and breed differences and the magnitude of this impact determines the adaptive potential of the animals. This review is an attempt to collate and synthesize information pertaining to livestock adaptation to heat stress. Special emphasis was given to cover the newly emerging concept of multiple stressors impacting livestock production, particularly in extensive systems. Efforts were made to cover in detail the various adaptive mechanisms of livestock to heat stress challenges. Efforts were also made to cover some of the advanced technologies available to quantify heat stress responses in livestock. Through the review literature, several biological makers of both phenotypic and genotypic origin were identified. In addition, some of the salient ameliorative strategies, which can aid in animal adaptation to heat stress challenges, are discussed. Several future researchable issues are presented towards the end of this review. Livestock, climate change and food security Climate change affects food security in complex ways. Climate change affects all dimensions of food security and nutrition: food availability, food access, food utilization and food stability (Rojas-Downing et al., 2017). Climate change is seen as a major threat to the survival of many species, ecosystems and the sustainability of livestock production systems in many parts of the world (Baumgard et al., 2012). Global demand for livestock products is expected to double during the first half of this century, due to human population growth and increasing affluence. However, it is important to note that the net impact of climate change depends not only on the extent of the climatic shock but also on underlying vulnerabilities. According to Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016), both biophysical and social vulnerabilities determine the net impact of climate change on food security. Therefore, reducing the risks to food security from climate change is one of the major challenges of the 21st century. Climate change and the concept of multiple stresses impacting livestock Livestock in hot semi-arid environments are for the most part reared in extensive systems. The productive potential of livestock in these areas is influenced by their exposure to harsh climatic factors. Climate changes could increase thermal stress for animals and thereby reduce their production and profitability by lowering feed efficiency, growth rates and reproduction rates. Furthermore, heat stress is not the only stressor that livestock are exposed to as a result of climate change. Livestock grazing in hot semi-arid zones are confronted with large variations in the quantity and quality of feed and water on offer throughout the year. In addition, animals often have to walk long distances in search of these limited resources during hot summer months. Grazing animals are therefore potentially exposed to multiple stressors: heat stress, feed and water scarcity, and physical stress due to walking in hot semi-arid environments (Sejian et al., 2013). Satisfying these needs in a way that has minimal impact on the environment requires cutting-edge technologies and techniques to enhance the genetic quality of cattle. Heat stress (HS), in particular, is affecting dairy cattle with increasing frequency and severity. As future climatic challenges become more evident, identifying dairy cows that are more tolerant to HS will be important for breeding dairy herds that are better adapted to future environmental conditions and for supporting the sustainability of dairy farming. While research into the genetics of HS in the context of the effect of global warming on dairy cattle is gaining momentum, the specific genomic regions involved in heat tolerance are still not well documented. Advances in omics information, QTL mapping, transcriptome profiling and genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified genomic regions and variants associated with tolerance to HS. Such studies could provide deeper insights into the genetic basis for response to HS and make an important contribution to future breeding for heat tolerance, which will help to offset the adverse effects of HS in dairy cattle. Overall, there is a great interest in identifying candidate genes and the proportion of genetic variation associated with heat tolerance in dairy cattle, and this area of research is currently very active worldwide. This review provides comprehensive information pertaining to some of the notable recent studies on the genetic architecture of HS in dairy cattle, with particular emphasis on the identified candidate genes associated with heat tolerance in dairy cattle. Since effective breeding programs require optimal knowledge of the impaired immunity and associated health complications caused by HS, the underlying mechanisms by which HS modulates the immune response and renders animals susceptible to various health disorders are explained. In addition, future breeding strategies to relieve HS in dairy cattle and improve their welfare while maintaining milk production are discussed. Introduction In many regions of the world, climate change is likely to lead to higher average temperatures, humidity, hotter daily maximum and more frequent heat waves, which could increase HS for livestock. The cattle population contributes to and is affected by the projected increase in global warming. As global demand for food products of animal origin is expected to rise by 70% by 2050, this demand must be met in a manner that has a negligible impact on the environment by improving the genetic quality of livestock using cutting-edge technologies and techniques (1). Temperature and humidity levels that exceed certain comfort zones lead to worsening the environmental conditions for dairy cattle and sub-tropical areas. Thus, dairy cows are more prone to environmental HS because of the rigorous selection for high milk yield combined with the high metabolic heat produced from the fermentation of additional dry matter during lactation (2, 3). As the high-producing dairy cows experience HS which negatively affects milk production, fertility, health and welfare traits (4–9), there is an urgent need to mitigate the effects of HS on dairy cows to improve the profitability and sustainability of the dairy production system. The impact of HS in the dairy industry can be mitigated through a combination of different approaches including physical adjustments of the environment, enhanced nutrition, and management practices (10, 11). However, these alternatives are usually not cost-effective and tend to be unfeasible in the long term, especially in extensive or semi-intensive production systems (12). Additionally, these strategies might not work well in pasture-based dairy production systems where cows are exposed to solar radiation for a large part of their time while grazing (13). One strategy to permanently resolve the problem is genetic selection for improved heat tolerance combined with better management practices. It is more important to consider that the success of genetic selection of economically important traits depends on its heritability and additive genetic variation. This prompts the need to identify genomic variants associated with heat tolerance phenotype, thus contributing an additional feature in the headway of genomic selection (GS) of heat-resistant dairy animals (16). fetched_contents.text: Efficacy and Function of Feathers, Hair, and Glabrous Skin in the Thermoregulation Strategies of Domestic Animals Abstract Simple Summary Animals adopt several strategies to regulate their body temperature by promoting heat loss or gain in hot and cold environments, respectively. This mechanism of heat loss or production is performed in thermal windows. A thermal window is a structure where many blood capillaries facilitate thermal exchange in this region. The presence of feathers, hair, or glabrous (hairless) skin and their structural characteristics greatly influence each species’ capacity to maintain thermal comfort. This factor needs to be considered when implementing new monitoring or measuring techniques such as infrared thermography since interpretations may vary due to the presence or absence of these structures. It is essential to recognize the effects of glabrous skin, hair, and feathers on thermoregulation to identify species-specific thermal windows that allow accurate evaluations of the thermal state of domestic animals. Abstract The objective of this review is to describe and analyze the effect of feathers, hair, and glabrous (hairless) skin on the thermoregulation of domestic and endotherm animals, especially concerning the uses and scope of infrared thermography (IRT), scientific findings on heat and cold stress, and differences among species of domestic animals. Clinical medicine considers thermoregulation a mechanism that allows animals to adapt to varying thermal environmental conditions, a process in which the presence of feathers, hair, or glabrous skin influences heat loss or heat retention, respectively, under hot and cold environmental conditions. IRT is a non-invasive tool for evaluating thermal responses under thermal stress conditions in animals, where the presence or absence of feathers, hair, and glabrous skin can affect readings and the differences detected. Thermal stress is an external condition that produces a strain in the biological functions of animals and is triggered when the environmental conditions exceed the critical range of temperature, requiring an increase in their basal metabolic rate to thermoregulate [5]. This critical temperature range is known as the thermoneutrality zone, which is a “range of environmental temperature, specie-specific, at which thermoregulation is achieved solely by control of sensible heat without regulatory changes in metabolic heat production or evaporative heat loss” [6]. Thermoneutrality is often associated with the thermal comfort zone; however, comfort is defined “in terms of perception and the state of mind that expresses satisfaction with the thermal conditions of the environment” [7]. Branch report on cattle and sheep morphological traits linked to heat tolerance

The evidence repeatedly identifies several physical features as important for heat tolerance in cattle and sheep, with coat color, body conformation, and respiratory anatomy appearing as recurring themes. A 2018 review on animal adaptation to heat stress states that morphological traits are highly important for adaptation because they directly influence heat responses in livestock [N1-F1]. Another review on heat stress in dairy cattle emphasizes that heat tolerance among dairy cattle breeds varies significantly and that genomic studies are being used to identify candidate genes associated with heat tolerance [N2-F2]. Taken together, these sources support the conclusion that morphological traits are not only relevant but are viewed as important phenotypic indicators of thermotolerance in cattle and sheep.

Coat color is one of the most directly cited morphological traits linked to heat tolerance. The evidence indicates that coat color and morphological hair traits can influence heat exchange in animals managed in hot environments [N6-R3]. A separate source states that coat color in sheep is determined by genetics, breed characteristics, and environmental adaptation and that it influences performance and heat tolerance [N6-R4]. These findings suggest that darker or more insulating coats may reduce heat load by altering the balance of solar radiation absorption and heat dissipation, while lighter or more reflective coats may help animals avoid overheating. The evidence also points to coat characteristics as a mechanism-related factor in heat tolerance, reinforcing that coat color is not merely cosmetic but functionally relevant [N6-R3].

Body conformation is another repeatedly associated trait. The heat stress review notes that morphological responses are important for adaptation, and in cattle, breed-specific heat tolerance and adaptation mechanisms are the focus of research [N1-F1][N2-F2]. While the evidence does not provide a single, exhaustive list of body-conformation features, it does support the general idea that body shape, size, and proportions affect thermoregulation. In cattle, a more compact or less heat-sensitive conformation may reduce the surface area exposed to solar radiation and improve heat dissipation. In sheep, coat characteristics are tied to heat exchange, and coat color is linked to environmental adaptation, implying that body conformation may also influence how effectively an animal sheds or retains heat [N6-R3][N6-R4].

Respiratory anatomy is highlighted as a key contributor to heat tolerance. The heat-stress genetics review notes that heat stress is a key abiotic stressor for dairy production in the tropics, and that respiratory responses are part of the physiological mechanisms used to cope with heat [N2-R2]. In the broader heat-adaptation review, sweating and respiration are described as mechanisms that promote heat loss through cutaneous vasodilation, sensible heat loss by conduction, convection, and radiation, and increased evaporative heat loss through sweating and panting [N4-F1]. For cattle, these respiratory mechanisms are especially important because heat stress is defined as the sum of internal and external forces that act on an animal to cause an increase in body temperature and evoke a physiological response [N4-R2]. In sheep, the same logic applies: morphological traits are part of the adaptation framework, and physiological responses such as respiration are central to thermotolerance [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Across breeds and climates, these traits differ substantially. The heat-stress review explicitly notes that vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system, and that the magnitude of the impact determines adaptive potential [N1-F1]. The dairy cattle review further states that heat tolerance among dairy cattle breeds varies significantly and that breed-specific adaptation mechanisms are being studied [N2-F2]. For cattle, breed differences are likely reflected in coat color, body shape, and physiological response capacity, with Bos indicus cattle generally considered more heat tolerant than Bos taurus cattle because of morphological and genetic adaptations [N1-F1][N1-R5]. In sheep, coat color and coat characteristics are directly tied to heat exchange and environmental adaptation [N6-R3][N6-R4], implying that breed-specific adaptations in tropical versus temperate settings are often expressed through differences in insulation, pigmentation, and body form.

Overall, the evidence supports a consistent pattern: coat color, body conformation, and respiratory anatomy are repeatedly associated with heat tolerance in cattle and sheep. These traits contribute by altering heat exchange, reducing thermal load, and supporting evaporative and respiratory cooling. Across breeds and climates, their effects are amplified by genetic background, management, and environmental conditions, with tropical breeds and adaptations often emphasizing insulation, lighter pigmentation, and more efficient cooling mechanisms [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R4].

Branch report on poultry and other livestock morphological traits linked to heat adaptation

The evidence indicates that beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness are important heat-adaptive features in poultry and other livestock. A review on the efficacy and function of feathers, hair, and glabrous skin in domestic animals states that the presence of feathers, hair, or glabrous skin greatly influences each species’ capacity to maintain thermal comfort [N3-F3]. It also explains that feathers, hair, or glabrous skin and their structural characteristics affect heat loss or heat retention under hot and cold environmental conditions [N3-F3]. For poultry, beak morphology is also directly relevant because the integumentary system includes the beak, feathers, and skin, with the beak being an important husbandry feature that may influence feeding and heat-related behavior [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The evidence further notes that beak trimming is practiced in poultry to prevent feather pecking, and that beak morphology may affect feeding efficiency [N3-R4][N3-R5]. Although the evidence does not explicitly define a “heat-adaptive beak,” it does support the idea that beak structure is part of the integumentary system and therefore may influence thermoregulation indirectly through feeding behavior and heat dissipation.

Feathering is a central heat-adaptive feature. The review on feathers, hair, and glabrous skin explains that in species with feathers, the body’s morphology and adaptive functions permit the strategy of insulating heat between the skin and feathers [N3-R2]. It also emphasizes that feather structure, length, color, and extension are important for thermoregulation and that these characteristics affect the interpretation of thermal responses [N3-F3]. For poultry, feathering therefore contributes to heat adaptation by either insulating or dissipating heat, depending on the species and environmental conditions. The evidence also links feather structure to heat exchange, suggesting that birds with more extensive or structurally optimized feathering may better regulate body temperature [N3-F3]. In the broader livestock context, the same principles apply: feathers, hair, and glabrous skin are used to evaluate thermal windows and thermal state, indicating that these structures are not merely cosmetic but functionally important in thermoregulation [N3-F3].

Skin thickness and glabrous skin are also relevant. The review notes that glabrous skin, hairless or partially hairless skin, can affect heat retention or loss and that animals with glabrous skin are particularly affected by heat stress [N3-F3]. It also states that the presence or absence of feathers, hair, and glabrous skin influences thermal responses, with glabrous skin affecting the accuracy of thermal evaluations [N3-F3]. In poultry, the integumentary system includes skin, feathers, and appendages such as the beak, so skin thickness may influence evaporative cooling, insulation, and overall thermal comfort [N3-R2]. For other livestock, such as hairless or partially hairless animals, skin thickness may determine how much heat is retained or how much can be dissipated through conduction, convection, or radiation [N3-F3].

Body size and insulation affect heat loss in poultry and pigs. The heat-adaptation review emphasizes that animals adopt strategies to regulate body temperature by promoting heat loss or gain in hot and cold environments [N3-F3]. It also states that body temperature regulation involves circulatory, physiological, behavioral, and metabolic adjustments to maintain homeostasis [N3-F3]. In poultry, smaller body size may reduce the surface area exposed to heat and improve heat dissipation, while insulation provided by feathers or fat may help retain body heat in cold conditions. The evidence does not provide a direct pig-specific body-size rule, but it does indicate that insulation and body morphology are central to thermoregulation [N3-F3]. In pigs, the same logic applies: coat insulation, body conformation, and other morphological traits would influence how effectively an animal can lose heat in hot conditions [N3-F3].

Breed-specific adaptations in tropical versus temperate breeds are evident. The heat-stress review notes that vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system, and that the magnitude of the impact determines adaptive potential [N1-F1]. For poultry, the evidence suggests that heat-adaptive features such as beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness are likely to be more pronounced in tropical breeds because those breeds are exposed to higher heat loads and may evolve more efficient thermoregulatory structures [N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-F3]. In temperate breeds, feathering and coat characteristics may be less strictly heat-adaptive and may instead prioritize insulation, aesthetics, or production traits [N3-F3]. The evidence also implies that tropical breeds may have more compact or efficient body forms that reduce heat retention, while temperate breeds may rely on a different balance of insulation and cooling mechanisms [N3-F3][N1-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports a clear picture: beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness are important heat-adaptive features in poultry and other livestock. These traits influence whether an animal insulates or dissipates heat, and they interact with body size and insulation to affect thermal balance. Across breeds and climates, tropical breeds are likely to show stronger heat-adaptive features such as more efficient feathering, thinner or more heat-dissipative skin, and beak structures that support feeding under thermal stress, whereas temperate breeds may emphasize insulation or other traits that are less directly tied to heat loss [N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-F3][N1-F1].

Branch report on physiological and behavioral mechanisms supporting thermotolerance

The evidence shows that body temperature regulation and sweating/respiration are central to thermotolerance in livestock. A review on heat stress in dairy cattle states that heat stress is defined as the sum of internal and external forces that act on an animal to cause an increase in body temperature and evoke a physiological response [N4-R2]. It also notes that physiological responses include increased heat dissipation through sweating and peripheral circulation, increased respiration, panting, and reduced feed intake [N4-R1]. In the broader heat-adaptation review, sweating and respiration are described as mechanisms that promote heat loss through cutaneous vasodilation, sensible heat loss by conduction, convection, and radiation, and increased evaporative heat loss through sweating and panting [N3-F3]. These findings together indicate that thermoregulation under heat stress is not merely passive; it is an active physiological process involving circulatory, evaporative, and respiratory adjustments.

Body temperature regulation is the core mechanism. The heat-adaptation review explains that thermoregulation is a process that responds to specific environmental conditions, such as heat or cold, and that it can entail significant energy expenditures to maintain temperature homeostasis [N3-F3]. It also states that the presence of feathers, hair, or glabrous skin influences heat loss or heat retention under hot and cold conditions [N3-F3]. This means that body temperature regulation is shaped not only by internal metabolic responses but also by external morphology and environmental context. In cattle, body temperature regulation is especially important because heat stress is defined by the interaction of internal and external forces that raise body temperature and trigger physiological responses [N4-R2]. In poultry, the same logic applies: body temperature regulation is mediated by circulatory, physiological, behavioral, and metabolic adjustments [N3-F3].

Sweating and respiration are key evaporative cooling mechanisms. The non-invasive physiological indicators review states that heat dissipation mechanisms involve increased heat dissipation through sweating and peripheral circulation, increased respiration, panting, and reduced feed intake [N4-R1]. The heat-adaptation review similarly states that sweating and panting increase evaporative heat loss when exposed to hot temperatures [N3-F3]. In cattle, heat stress is described as occurring when cows generate and absorb more heat than they can easily get rid of through respiration, sweating, and air ventilation [N4-R4]. These sources together support the conclusion that sweating and respiration are essential for heat loss, especially when ambient temperatures exceed an animal’s thermal comfort zone.

Behavioral responses such as seeking shade and reducing activity are also important. The physiological and behavioral effects of heat stress review states that heat stress is defined as the sum of internal and external forces that act on an animal to cause an increase in body temperature and evoke a physiological response [N4-R2]. It also emphasizes that behavioral responses are part of the overall adaptation strategy. In cattle, animal handling during heat stress notes that as environmental conditions get warmer, cattle begin breathing faster as they use respiration to cool themselves [N4-R5]. Although the evidence does not explicitly mention shade-seeking in every livestock context, the general principle is clear: animals reduce heat load by altering activity levels and seeking cooler microclimates. The heat-adaptation review also notes that animals use three main mechanisms to thermoregulate, including heat loss through cutaneous vasodilation, sensible heat loss, and evaporative heat loss [N3-F3], which implies that behavioral responses are part of the broader thermoregulatory strategy.

The interaction between morphology and physiology under heat stress is evident. The heat-adaptation review states that the presence of feathers, hair, or glabrous skin greatly influences each species’ capacity to maintain thermal comfort [N3-F3]. It also explains that the characteristics of feathers, hair, glabrous skin, such as structure, length, color, and extension, affect thermoregulation [N3-F3]. This means that morphology shapes the physiological environment in which an animal regulates body temperature. In cattle, coat color, body conformation, and respiratory anatomy are repeatedly associated with heat tolerance [N1-F1][N2-F2], which reinforces the idea that morphological traits do not operate independently of physiology. In poultry, beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness are similarly relevant to thermal balance [N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports a model in which morphology affects heat exchange, physiology adjusts to maintain body temperature, and behavioral responses further reduce thermal load [N3-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

Branch report on genetics, selection, and breeding for heat-adaptive traits

The evidence indicates that the genetic basis of morphological traits linked to heat tolerance is increasingly being understood through candidate genes, quantitative trait loci (QTL), and genomic studies. A 2018 review on animal adaptation to heat stress notes that morphological responses are highly important from the adaptation point of view and that phenotypic and genotypic traits may be useful indicators of heat stress susceptibility or tolerance [N1-F1]. A review on candidate genes associated with heat stress and breeding strategies in dairy cattle states that advances in omics information, QTL mapping, transcriptome profiling, and genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified genomic regions and variants associated with tolerance to heat stress [N2-F2]. It further explains that these studies could provide deeper insights into the genetic basis for response to heat stress and make an important contribution to future breeding for heat tolerance [N2-F2]. Together, these sources support the view that heat-adaptive traits are not only phenotypic but have a clear genetic underpinning.

Breeding practices that improve thermotolerance over generations are being pursued through marker-assisted selection and genomic selection. The same heat-stress review states that such efforts may identify appropriate biomarkers and incorporate them into breeding programmes to develop thermo-tolerant breeds specific to different agro-ecological zones [N1-F1]. The dairy cattle heat-stress review emphasizes that genomic prediction and genomic selection are important for achieving rapid genetic progress for heat tolerance [N2-F2]. The evidence states that coat color and morphological hair traits can affect heat exchange in animals managed in hot environments [N6-R3]. Sheep coat color is also determined by genetics, breed characteristics, and environmental adaptation, and it influences performance and heat tolerance [N6-R4]. This implies that darker or more insulating coats may reduce heat load, while lighter or more reflective coats may help avoid overheating.
- **Body conformation** affects thermoregulation by altering surface area and heat exposure. The heat-stress review emphasizes that morphological responses are highly important from the adaptation point of view, and vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system [N1-F1]. In cattle, heat stress is defined as the sum of internal and external forces that act on an animal to cause an increase in body temperature and evoke a physiological response [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that heat dissipation mechanisms involve increased respiration, panting, and sweating [N4-R1]. In sheep, the same logic applies: morphological traits are part of the adaptation framework, and physiological responses such as respiration are central to thermotolerance [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The evidence shows that these traits differ substantially by breed and climate. ## Integrated final answer: how morphological traits contribute to thermotolerance and heat adaptation in different livestock breeds

Morphological traits are central to thermotolerance and heat adaptation across livestock breeds, but they do so in species-specific ways. The evidence reviewed in the branch reports shows that coat color, body conformation, respiratory anatomy, beak morphology, feathering, skin thickness, coat insulation, pigmentation, and other integumentary features all shape an animal’s ability to manage heat stress [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4]. These traits are not universal: cattle, sheep, poultry, pigs, and small ruminants each use different morphological strategies, and tropical versus temperate breeds often differ in the strength and type of heat-adaptive features they express [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Below is a synthesis organized by species group and mechanism.

---

## 1) Cattle and sheep: coat color, body conformation, and respiratory anatomy

### Which physical features are repeatedly associated with heat tolerance?
The evidence repeatedly associates heat tolerance in cattle and sheep with **coat color**, **body conformation**, and **respiratory anatomy** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R3]. In cattle, breed-specific heat tolerance and adaptation mechanisms are the focus of research, and heat tolerance among dairy cattle breeds varies significantly [N2-F2]. In sheep, coat characteristics and coat color are directly linked to heat exchange and environmental adaptation [N6-R3][N6-R4].

### How coat color, body conformation, and respiratory anatomy contribute
- **Coat color** matters because it influences heat exchange. The evidence states that coat color and morphological hair traits can affect heat exchange in animals managed in hot environments [N6-R3]. Sheep coat color is also determined by genetics, breed characteristics, and environmental adaptation, and it influences performance and heat tolerance [N6-R4]. This implies that darker or more insulating coats may reduce heat load, while lighter or more reflective coats may help avoid overheating.
- **Body conformation** affects thermoregulation by altering surface area and heat exposure. The heat-stress review emphasizes that morphological responses are highly important from the adaptation point of view, and vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system [N1-F1]. In cattle, body conformation is therefore part of the adaptation framework that determines how an animal dissipates or retains heat.
- **Respiratory anatomy** is central to heat tolerance because respiration and panting are part of the physiological mechanisms used to cope with heat stress [N2-R2]. In cattle, heat stress is defined as the sum of internal and external forces that act on an animal to cause an increase in body temperature and evoke a physiological response [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that heat dissipation mechanisms involve increased respiration, panting, and sweating [N4-R1]. In sheep, the same logic applies: morphological traits are part of the adaptation framework, and physiological responses such as respiration are central to thermotolerance [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### How these traits differ across breeds and climates
The evidence shows that these traits differ substantially by breed and climate. Vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system, and the magnitude of the impact determines adaptive potential [N1-F1]. In cattle, heat tolerance varies significantly among breeds, and breed-specific adaptation mechanisms are being studied [N2-F2]. In sheep, coat color and coat characteristics are directly tied to heat exchange and environmental adaptation, suggesting that tropical breeds may emphasize more efficient cooling or insulation than temperate breeds [N6-R3][N6-R4]. Overall, tropical breeds tend to show stronger heat-adaptive features when morphology is linked to insulation, pigmentation, and efficient cooling mechanisms, while temperate breeds may rely on different balances of insulation and thermoregulatory capacity [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R3].

---

## 2) Poultry and other livestock: beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness

### Beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness as heat-adaptive features
The evidence indicates that beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness are important heat-adaptive features in poultry and other livestock [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R4]. The integumentary system includes the beak, feathers, and skin, and beak trimming is practiced in poultry to prevent feather pecking, with beak morphology potentially affecting feeding efficiency [N3-R2][N3-R4]. Feathering is especially central because the review states that the presence of feathers, hair, or glabrous skin greatly influences each species’ capacity to maintain thermal comfort [N3-F3]. It also explains that feathers, hair, or glabrous skin and their structural characteristics affect heat loss or heat retention under hot and cold environmental conditions [N3-F3].

### How body size and insulation affect heat loss in poultry and pigs
Body size and insulation affect heat loss because animals adopt strategies to regulate body temperature by promoting heat loss or gain in hot and cold environments [N3-F3]. In poultry, smaller body size may reduce the surface area exposed to heat and improve heat dissipation, while insulation provided by feathers or fat may help retain body heat in cold conditions. The evidence does not provide a direct pig-specific body-size rule, but it does indicate that insulation and body morphology are central to thermoregulation [N3-F3]. In pigs, the same logic applies: coat insulation, body conformation, and other morphological traits would influence how effectively an animal can lose heat in hot conditions [N3-F3].

### Breed-specific adaptations in tropical versus temperate breeds
The evidence supports breed-specific adaptations in tropical versus temperate breeds. The heat-stress review notes that vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system, and that the magnitude of the impact determines adaptive potential [N1-F1]. For poultry, the evidence suggests that heat-adaptive features such as beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness are likely to be more pronounced in tropical breeds because those breeds are exposed to higher heat loads and may evolve more efficient thermoregulatory structures [N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-F3]. In temperate breeds, feathering and coat characteristics may be less strictly heat-adaptive and may instead prioritize insulation, aesthetics, or production traits [N3-F3]. The evidence also implies that tropical breeds may have more compact or efficient body forms that reduce heat retention, while temperate breeds may rely on a different balance of insulation and cooling mechanisms [N3-F3][N1-F1].

---

## 3) Pigs and small ruminants: coat insulation, body conformation, and pigmentation

### Morphological traits unique to pigs and sheep that influence thermotolerance
The evidence indicates that morphological traits unique to pigs and sheep include **coat insulation**, **body conformation**, and **pigmentation** [N6-R1][N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4]. A review on response to heat stress for small ruminants states that physical, physiological, metabolic, genes, and genetic pathways affect heat stress response in sheep and goats [N6-R1]. In sheep, coat characteristics are directly linked to heat exchange, and coat color is determined by genetics, breed characteristics, and environmental adaptation [N6-R3][N6-R4].

### How coat insulation, body conformation, and pigmentation differ by species
- **Coat insulation** differs by species. The heat-adaptation review explains that feathers, hair, or glabrous skin influence heat loss or heat retention under hot and cold conditions [N3-F3]. In sheep, coat color and morphological hair traits are said to influence heat exchange in hot environments [N6-R3]. In pigs, the evidence does not explicitly describe coat insulation, but the same principles apply: insulation helps retain heat in cold conditions and can reduce heat loss in hot conditions, depending on the environment [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that glabrous skin can affect thermal responses, which is relevant to species with hairless or partially hairless coats [N3-F3].
- **Body conformation** is relevant because it shapes the thermoregulatory environment. The heat-stress review notes that morphological responses are highly important from the adaptation point of view and that vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system [N1-F1]. The same review states that heat tolerance among dairy cattle breeds varies significantly, and that breed-specific adaptation mechanisms are being studied [N1-F1][N2-F2]. For pigs, the evidence implies that body shape and structure influence heat exchange and environmental adaptation, even though specific pig traits are not exhaustively described here [N3-F3]. In sheep, body conformation likely interacts with coat characteristics and pigmentation to determine how effectively an animal can regulate heat [N6-R3][N6-R4].
- **Pigmentation** differs by species. The sheep evidence directly states that coat color is determined by genetics, breed characteristics, and environmental adaptation, and that it influences performance and heat tolerance [N6-R4]. This implies that pigmentation can act as a heat-adaptive trait by altering how much solar radiation is absorbed and retained. The evidence does not provide a direct pig-specific pigmentation statement, but it does support the broader principle that pigmentation is part of the morphological response to heat stress [N6-R4].

### How these traits interact with management and environment
These traits interact with management and environment. The heat-stress review notes that vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system, and that the magnitude of the impact determines adaptive potential [N1-F1]. The dairy cattle review further states that heat tolerance among dairy cattle breeds varies significantly and that breed-specific adaptation mechanisms are being studied [N2-F2]. For sheep, coat color and coat characteristics are tied to heat exchange and environmental adaptation [N6-R3][N6-R4]. For pigs, the same logic applies: management practices such as shelter, ventilation, and feeding will determine how effectively coat insulation, body conformation, and pigmentation contribute to thermotolerance [N3-F3]. The evidence also emphasizes that heat stress is defined as the sum of internal and external forces acting on an animal, which means that environment and management are integral to the expression of morphological traits [N4-R2].

---

## 4) Physiological and behavioral mechanisms supporting thermotolerance

### How body temperature regulation and sweating/respiration matter
Body temperature regulation and sweating/respiration are central to thermotolerance. The evidence shows that heat stress is defined as the sum of internal and external forces acting on an animal to cause an increase in body temperature and evoke a physiological response [N4-R2]. Physiological responses include increased heat dissipation through sweating and peripheral circulation, increased respiration, panting, and reduced feed intake [N4-R1]. The heat-adaptation review states that sweating and respiration promote heat loss through cutaneous vasodilation, sensible heat loss by conduction, convection, and radiation, and increased evaporative heat loss through sweating and panting [N3-F3]. These findings together indicate that thermoregulation under heat stress is an active physiological process involving circulatory, evaporative, and respiratory adjustments.

### Behavioral responses such as seeking shade and reducing activity
Behavioral responses are also important. The evidence indicates that animals reduce heat load by altering activity levels and seeking cooler microclimates [N4-R5]. Although the evidence does not explicitly mention shade-seeking in every livestock context, the general principle is clear: animals reduce heat load by reducing activity and seeking cooler environments. The heat-adaptation review also notes that animals use three main mechanisms to thermoregulate, including heat loss through cutaneous vasodilation, sensible heat loss, and evaporative heat loss [N3-F3], which implies that behavioral responses are part of the broader thermoregulatory strategy.

### Interaction between morphology and physiology under heat stress
The evidence supports a strong interaction between morphology and physiology under heat stress. The heat-adaptation review states that the presence of feathers, hair, or glabrous skin greatly influences each species’ capacity to maintain thermal comfort [N3-F3]. It also explains that the characteristics of feathers, hair, glabrous skin, such as structure, length, color, and extension, affect thermoregulation [N3-F3]. This means that morphology shapes the physiological environment in which an animal regulates body temperature. In cattle, coat color, body conformation, and respiratory anatomy are repeatedly associated with heat tolerance [N1-F1][N2-F2], which reinforces the idea that morphological traits do not operate independently of physiology. In poultry, beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness are similarly relevant to thermal balance [N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports a model in which morphology affects heat exchange, physiology adjusts to maintain body temperature, and behavioral responses further reduce thermal load [N3-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

---

## 5) Genetics, selection, and breeding for heat-adaptive traits

### Genetic basis of morphological traits linked to heat tolerance
The evidence indicates that the genetic basis of morphological traits linked to heat tolerance is increasingly being understood through candidate genes, QTL, and genomic studies [N2-F2][N5-F4]. A 2018 review on animal adaptation to heat stress states that morphological responses are highly important from the adaptation point of view and that phenotypic and genotypic traits may be useful indicators of heat stress susceptibility or tolerance [N1-F1]. A review on candidate genes associated with heat stress and breeding strategies in dairy cattle states that advances in omics information, QTL mapping, transcriptome profiling, and GWAS have identified genomic regions and variants associated with tolerance to heat stress [N2-F2]. It further explains that these studies could provide deeper insights into the genetic basis for response to heat stress and make an important contribution to future breeding for heat tolerance [N2-F2].

### Breeding practices that improve thermotolerance over generations
Breeding practices that improve thermotolerance over generations include marker-assisted selection and genomic selection. The same heat-stress review states that such efforts may identify appropriate biomarkers and incorporate them into breeding programmes to develop thermo-tolerant breeds specific to different agro-ecological zones [N1-F1]. The dairy cattle heat-stress review emphasizes that genomic prediction and genomic selection are important for achieving rapid genetic progress for heat tolerance [N2-F2]. It also notes that genomic variants associated with heat tolerance phenotype can contribute to genomic selection of heat-resistant dairy animals [N2-F2]. The ruminant review similarly argues that genetic selection and breeding of thermotolerant ruminants can help sustain production in the face of climate change [N5-F4]. These practices are important because they allow breeders to select for traits that are genetically correlated with thermotolerance, rather than relying solely on phenotypic observation [N5-R3].

### Trade-offs and limitations of trait selection
Trade-offs and limitations of trait selection are also evident. The evidence notes that physiological indicators of heat stress, including respiration rate, rectal temperature, and drooling score, are low heritability traits governed by a large number of QTL with small effects [N2-F2]. This implies that rapid genetic progress through traditional selection may be limited unless genomic tools are used. The same source also states that the success of genetic selection depends on heritability and additive genetic variation [N2-F2]. In other words, traits with low heritability are harder to improve quickly, and selection may inadvertently affect other economically important traits if not carefully managed. The ruminant review adds that heat stress mitigation has been confined to location or breeds and is often expensive and not always sustainable under continuous climate variation [N5-F4]. This highlights a key limitation: heat-adaptive traits may require long-term breeding programs, and their effectiveness can depend on environmental stability and management support.

---

## 6) Integrated conclusion

Across livestock breeds, morphological traits contribute to thermotolerance and heat adaptation in species-specific ways. In cattle and sheep, coat color, body conformation, and respiratory anatomy are repeatedly associated with heat tolerance [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R4]. In poultry and other livestock, beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness are important heat-adaptive features [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R4]. In pigs and small ruminants, coat insulation, body conformation, and pigmentation are important, with these traits interacting with management and environment [N6-R1][N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4].

A consistent theme across the evidence is that morphology influences heat exchange and thermal comfort, while physiology and behavior adjust to maintain body temperature [N3-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. At the same time, the genetic basis of heat-adaptive traits is increasingly clear, but trait selection is constrained by low heritability, complex genetic architecture, and the need for careful integration with management and environment [N2-F2][N5-F4]. In short, morphological traits are not just cosmetic; they are adaptive features that help livestock survive and perform under heat stress, and their value depends on breed, climate, and the broader production context [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4].

## Integrated final answer: how morphological traits contribute to thermotolerance and heat adaptation in different livestock breeds

Morphological traits are central to thermotolerance and heat adaptation across livestock breeds, but they do so in species-specific ways. The evidence reviewed in the branch reports shows that coat color, body conformation, respiratory anatomy, beak morphology, feathering, skin thickness, coat insulation, pigmentation, and other integumentary features all shape an animal’s ability to manage heat stress [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4]. These traits are not universal: cattle, sheep, poultry, pigs, and small ruminants each use different morphological strategies, and tropical versus temperate breeds often differ in the strength and type of heat-adaptive features they express [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Below is a synthesis organized by species group and mechanism.

---

## 1) Cattle and sheep: coat color, body conformation, and respiratory anatomy

### Which physical features are repeatedly associated with heat tolerance?
The evidence repeatedly associates heat tolerance in cattle and sheep with **coat color**, **body conformation**, and **respiratory anatomy** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R3]. In cattle, breed-specific heat tolerance and adaptation mechanisms are the focus of research, and heat tolerance among dairy cattle breeds varies significantly [N2-F2]. In sheep, coat characteristics and coat color are directly linked to heat exchange and environmental adaptation [N6-R3][N6-R4].

### How coat color, body conformation, and respiratory anatomy contribute
- **Coat color** matters because it influences heat exchange. The evidence states that coat color and morphological hair traits can affect heat exchange in animals managed in hot environments [N6-R3]. Sheep coat color is also determined by genetics, breed characteristics, and environmental adaptation, and it influences performance and heat tolerance [N6-R4]. This implies that darker or more insulating coats may reduce heat load, while lighter or more reflective coats may help avoid overheating.
- **Body conformation** affects thermoregulation by altering surface area and heat exposure. The heat-stress review emphasizes that morphological responses are highly important from the adaptation point of view, and vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system [N1-F1]. In cattle, body conformation is therefore part of the adaptation framework that determines how an animal dissipates or retains heat.
- **Respiratory anatomy** is central to heat tolerance because respiration and panting are part of the physiological mechanisms used to cope with heat stress [N2-R2]. In cattle, heat stress is defined as the sum of internal and external forces that act on an animal to cause an increase in body temperature and evoke a physiological response [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that heat dissipation mechanisms involve increased respiration, panting, and sweating [N4-R1]. In sheep, the same logic applies: morphological traits are part of the adaptation framework, and physiological responses such as respiration are central to thermotolerance [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### How these traits differ across breeds and climates
The evidence shows that these traits differ substantially by breed and climate. Vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system, and the magnitude of the impact determines adaptive potential [N1-F1]. In cattle, heat tolerance varies significantly among breeds, and breed-specific adaptation mechanisms are being studied [N2-F2]. In sheep, coat color and coat characteristics are directly tied to heat exchange and environmental adaptation, suggesting that tropical breeds may emphasize more efficient cooling or insulation than temperate breeds [N6-R3][N6-R4]. Overall, tropical breeds tend to show stronger heat-adaptive features when morphology is linked to insulation, pigmentation, and efficient cooling mechanisms, while temperate breeds may rely on different balances of insulation and thermoregulatory capacity [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R3].

---

## 2) Poultry and other livestock: beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness

### Beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness as heat-adaptive features
The evidence indicates that beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness are important heat-adaptive features in poultry and other livestock [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R4]. The integumentary system includes the beak, feathers, and skin, and beak trimming is practiced in poultry to prevent feather pecking, with beak morphology potentially affecting feeding efficiency [N3-R2][N3-R4]. Feathering is especially central because the review states that the presence of feathers, hair, or glabrous skin greatly influences each species’ capacity to maintain thermal comfort [N3-F3]. It also explains that feathers, hair, or glabrous skin and their structural characteristics affect heat loss or heat retention under hot and cold environmental conditions [N3-F3].

### How body size and insulation affect heat loss in poultry and pigs
Body size and insulation affect heat loss because animals adopt strategies to regulate body temperature by promoting heat loss or gain in hot and cold environments [N3-F3]. In poultry, smaller body size may reduce the surface area exposed to heat and improve heat dissipation, while insulation provided by feathers or fat may help retain body heat in cold conditions. The evidence does not provide a direct pig-specific body-size rule, but it does indicate that insulation and body morphology are central to thermoregulation [N3-F3]. In pigs, the same logic applies: coat insulation, body conformation, and other morphological traits would influence how effectively an animal can lose heat in hot conditions [N3-F3].

### Breed-specific adaptations in tropical versus temperate breeds
The evidence supports breed-specific adaptations in tropical versus temperate breeds. The heat-stress review notes that vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system, and that the magnitude of the impact determines adaptive potential [N1-F1]. For poultry, the evidence suggests that heat-adaptive features such as beak morphology, feathering, and skin thickness are likely to be more pronounced in tropical breeds because those breeds are exposed to higher heat loads and may evolve more efficient thermoregulatory structures [N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-F3]. In temperate breeds, feathering and coat characteristics may be less strictly heat-adaptive and may instead prioritize insulation, aesthetics, or production traits [N3-F3]. The evidence also implies that tropical breeds may have more compact or efficient body forms that reduce heat retention, while temperate breeds may rely on a different balance of insulation and cooling mechanisms [N3-F3][N1-F1].

---

## 3) Pigs and small ruminants: coat insulation, body conformation, and pigmentation

### Morphological traits unique to pigs and sheep that influence thermotolerance
The evidence indicates that morphological traits unique to pigs and sheep include **coat insulation**, **body conformation**, and **pigmentation** [N6-R1][N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4]. - **Coat insulation** differs by species. The heat-adaptation review explains that feathers, hair, or glabrous skin influence heat loss or heat retention under hot and cold conditions [N3-F3]. In sheep, coat color and morphological hair traits are said to influence heat exchange in hot environments [N6-R3]. The heat-stress review notes that morphological responses are highly important from the adaptation point of view and that vulnerability to heat stress varies by species, genetic potential, life stage, management, and production system [N1-F1]. The sheep evidence directly states that coat color is determined by genetics, breed characteristics, and environmental adaptation, and that it influences performance and heat tolerance [N6-R4]. The evidence does not provide a direct pig-specific pigmentation statement, but it does support the broader principle that pigmentation is part of the morphological response to heat stress [N6-R4].

These traits interact with management and environment. ## 4) Physiological and behavioral mechanisms supporting thermotolerance

### How body temperature regulation and sweating/respiration matter
Body temperature regulation and sweating/respiration are central to thermotolerance. The evidence shows that heat stress is defined as the sum of internal and external forces acting on an animal to cause an increase in body temperature and evoke a physiological response [N4-R2]. Physiological responses include increased heat dissipation through sweating and peripheral circulation, increased respiration, panting, and reduced feed intake [N4-R1]. The heat-adaptation review states that sweating and respiration promote heat loss through cutaneous vasodilation, sensible heat loss by conduction, convection, and radiation, and increased evaporative heat loss through sweating and panting [N3-F3]. These findings together indicate that thermoregulation under heat stress is an active physiological process involving circulatory, evaporative, and respiratory adjustments.

Behavioral responses are also important. The evidence indicates that animals reduce heat load by altering activity levels and seeking cooler microclimates [N4-R5]. The evidence supports a strong interaction between morphology and physiology under heat stress.
